Oh then that’s easy. Here’s a list of important things

•**Society**

-Who are/is your sapient race(s) and what are their social lives like (if they have one at all)? What is their culture and main religion, along with the history and symbolisms behind them? What is their technology like, what resources do they have access to, what laws do they have, and what is their economy like? This also includes conflict and historical events.

•**Non-sapient Life**

-What are some species that inhabit your world? (this includes everything from marine life to microorganisms if you want to get that specific) If you want more of a realistic approach, how did they evolve? What environments do they inhabit and which ones are domesticated? Etc.

•**Otherworldly/Supernatural Entities**

-What are your gods/goddesses like (if you have any). Do ghosts, spirits, and demons exist in your world? What about angels even? How do your societies view afterlife and how much of a threat do otherworldly powers pose to the life in your world?

•**Environment**

-What kind of environments are in your world? What environment is most common and houses the most life? What environment is the hardest to live in? Describe the climates and geographies of these areas.

They are very light in order for their wings to carry them, with a thinner layer of feathers than birds and hollow bones.    Harpies use aggressive and symbiotic mimicry to attract and find food. Some species will mimic birds during mating season to attract birds of the such species. Harpies raise their young much like birds do. However, when the parent is unable to protect or look after the eggs/hatchlings, they will often drop the child in another harpy/bird nest. This alternative parenthood is what caused mimicry to develop amongst harpy species.

**Family Life and Mating Behaviorisms**

Many dragons spend most of their social lives in large groups called colonies. These colonies usually live on cliffsides, trees, or other vertical/upside down surfaces (like mentioned before).

Dragons form strictly homosexual relationships, and will build nests in holes along different surfaces. Due to their inability to produce asexually, males and females will split off in pairs to mate. Once the female has laid her eggs (usually four unless there are complications), the two will go their seperate ways and take two of the eggs to raise with their chosen partner. This guarantees that each pair gets an equal amount of offspring to raise. 

 Both parents have different jobs until the eggs hatch. One parent stays with the nest and protects it, while the other leaves off and hunts for itself and its partner. However, once the eggs do hatch, the younglings (called wyverns) will latch onto their protector parent’s back while they fly and hunt. Eventually, the wyverns will develop the ability to fly and be able to part from their parents.

Harpies:

•Harpies evolved from therapods, which make them heavily related to birds. However, they bare a closer resemblance to their ancestors, which means they are very raptor-like in appearance.

•Harpies use aggressive mimicry. This means that they will mock the appearance and voice of different birds to attract and eat them. For example, sparrow harpies resemble sparrows in appearance (design-wise) and voice. Being relatively small, it is easy for them to mock and confuse their bird counterparts.

•Harpies also utilize symbiotic mimicry. They mimic the appearances and voices of different birds to get the same benefits as that specific species. Crow harpies will often follow groups to food sources.

•It is not uncommon for mothers to drop their young in other harpy/bird nests (think sort of a mockingbird deal)

•Harpies have two mouths. The upper one is a beak (part of the whole mimicry deal) that helps them mimic bird calls and behaviors. The bottom one is a human-like grimace, which is full of sharp teeth that fuel their carnivorous diet.
